extracted.intended_audience: writers, students, and readers interested in symbolism in art and literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and conceptual criteria for identifying, creating, and interpreting artistic symbols (concrete elements that suggest deeper, non-literal meanings) across literature and visual art. Useful for authors crafting symbols and readers/scholars analyzing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of an artistic symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: A symbol is a concrete element like an object, character, image, situation, or action that suggests or hints at abstract, deeper, or non-literal meanings or ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete elements in a work (objects, characters, images, situations, actions) to point beyond their literal meaning; consider the element's literal role and the additional meanings it may suggest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowed forms/types of symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols may be an object, a person/character, an image, a situation, or an action; writing itself is inherently a system of symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating or identifying symbols, look across modes (visual, literary, poetic) — synonyms include visual symbol, literary symbol, poetic symbol. Any element of the artwork can function symbolically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolism as a narrative device (intentionality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Artistic symbols may be intentionally built into a work by its creator, making symbolism a deliberate narrative device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors can deliberately embed symbols to reinforce theme or character; when evaluating, consider authorial choices and how a symbol aligns with narrative intent and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolism as reader/scholar interpretation (interpretive emergence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols may also be decided upon by the audience or by a consensus of scholars through their interpretation of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that symbolic meaning can emerge post-creation; multiple valid interpretations can arise from reader response and critical discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-fixed, suggestive nature of symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols generally do not 'stand for' any one meaning, nor for anything absolutely definite; they point, they hint, or, as Henry James put it, they 'cast long shadows'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating symbols as one-to-one signifiers; allow for ambiguity and layered meanings when creating or analyzing symbolism; consider multiple possible readings rather than enforcing a single definitive meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish cultural/common symbols from work-specific symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Some symbolism recurs within or across cultures (e.g., a rose symbolizes beauty; a lion symbolizes strength), while other symbols recur only in the context of one particular work (e.g., blood in Macbeth symbolizes violent behavior and guilt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting or devising symbols, assess whether the symbol draws on widely shared cultural associations or is established and developed uniquely within the text/artwork; context matters for which associations will be accessible or persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color symbolism as a category
rubrics_metrics.description: Color symbolism is a specific instance of symbolism (for example, certain colors symbolize national flags and, by extension, nations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to color choices as potential symbolic shorthand; consider cultural color associations and the specific visual/textual context to infer meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of concrete examples to ground symbolic reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples such as the bespectacled eyes on a billboard in The Great Gatsby being interpreted as symbolizing the gaze of God illustrate how specific images can be read symbolically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use illustrative examples from literature and art to model how concrete elements map onto abstract interpretations; when teaching or learning symbolism, analyze canonical examples to see how symbolism operates in practice.
